questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a German speaking country, as I saw the study exchange as an ideal opportunity for improving my language skills. I didn't have a lot choice: Zürich or Munich. I chose Munich mostly because of my gut feelings, and I didn't regret it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The Technical University of Munich is a very good university in my opinion. It however has a very misleading name, as not all of it schools are locate in Munich. I was at the School of Life Sciences, which is located 30 min north of Munich in a little town called Freising. This shouldn't nevertheless hold you from applying to the school. The campus is amazing: very green, cute and everyone knows each other. You therefore quickly become a part of the student life at campus. Freising is also very nice. It is mainly inhabited by students and is far from dead and boring. So many events all the time! Bierfest, Nacht der Musik, and many other celebrations. You'll get the true bavarian experience by living in Freising. Most exchange students lived in Freising itself and not Munich, which I would really recommend.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was honestly a very stressful application process, which made me regret the destination choice big time before my departure. The administration at TUM was clearly understaffed and directly asked us not to send to emails. Moreover, my contact person didn't anser me for several months despite my many mails concerning very important steps in the application process.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had one introduction lecture at our campus. Apart from that, we were very much alone as exchange students, but we help and support each other, and it turned out to be great.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
You can apply for a room in some of the dorms in Freising or Munich, but I didn't get one. I had to find a room on the private market. Here are my recommendations:
- start three to two months in advance
- go to WG-gesucht, which is a platform for finding shared apartments. Make a personal and a little original profile, and write your messages in German (if possible). 
- be fast 
- I went to Munich 3 days two months before the semester start, to see the rooms personally (there is a risk of being scammed). It works well to write, that you are in the town and willing to see the room same day.
- I paid 600€ for a room in a house with 6 other people. I have the impression that the price was kind of average for Freising.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Freising is really small so you pretty much will on campus no matter what. 

If you want to live in Munich, you have to take to train to get to Freising. It takes 25 min with the regional train and 45 with the S-train. Be aware of Deutsche Bahn's reputation of being unpunctual!!!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The choice of courses was definitely the most confusing and stressful. Before your arrival, you have to choose courses based on the old catalogues from the previous study years. You have no chance what so ever to know whether the courses will be offered, and neither has the university. My contact person didn't want to sign my Online Learning Agreement before I had a list of courses that will be offered. I therefore personally had to write to five professors to ask them whether their courses will be offered. 

When I finally arrived on campus, no authorities could help me with registrering for the courses. It turned out, that the students normally just register to plenty of courses, try them out, and just don't register for the exams, if they don't like the course. It was much more chill, than the administration made it sound like. I would have loved, that someone had told me that during the application process.

The registration period varies from course to course (it depends on the professors). You therefore ave to be very organised to not miss the registration periods. However, I have the impression that the profeessor are pretty tolerant, and would let you join if you wrote to them.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: nothing...

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I ended up taking six courses. The courses are pretty small: some were 3 credits, other 5 credits. Because of their weird registration process, the classes were in general very small. We were for instance only 4 students showing up for some of the courses, so we almost got private lessons. 

The most difficult part was to make a schedule that made sense with no overlaps between the six classes. It took me many evenings. 

I would recommend to choose some courses that have the exams during the semester. Otherwise you'll end up with having six exams on few weeks.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Technical University Munich seems very disorganised compare to UCPH, because the organisation is decentralised. The professors are doing their things, and the adminisatrion has no control over it. This is annoying when you are in Denmark trying to understand he structure, but as soon as you are there, it is much easier to ask for help or get influence on the course and even the exam date. It makes everything more flexible and the contact to the professors is ok easy. I for instance forgot to register for one exam before the deadline. I just wrote to the professor and he registered me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Because each class has few credits, you can choose many different classes. Very nice!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is fine. The classes were very interesting.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
They really like lectures and weird (unnecessary in my opinion) details. In general, the professor are very dedicated and teach about their own research.

I was also impressed about the dedication of the students. They were in cereal very active in the classes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Modern topics in Evolutionary Biology (5 ECTS)
- Nutrition and Microbe-Host Interactions (5 ECTS)
- Applied Microbiology (ECTS)
- German as foreign language (8 ECTS)
- Hot Topics: Recent Advances in Immunology and Infectious Diseases (3ECTS)
- Transgenic and Stem Cell Biotechnology (5 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
- Modern topics in Evolutionary Biology (5 ECTS)
almost philosophical. You learn to read research papers about evolution written by biologist in cooperation with philosophers. It requires a lot of work though, and the exam is a three hour essay where you have to answer a complex question based on several research papers that you read in advance.

- Nutrition and Microbe-Host Interactions (5 ECTS)
Held by Dirk Haller, that has been working with the gut microbiome for 25 years! He's very cool. You can choose a lab or bioinformatic track. I took the bioinformatic track where we had to analyse sequencing data from our own stool samples. Also very cool.

- Applied Microbiology (ECTS)
I was struggling here. I didn't have a lot of basics for understanding and there was a lot of biochemistry. But interesting. 

- German as foreign language (8 ECTS)
Really nice. The teacher was sweet and so was the rest of the class. It was a good break from the other classes.

- Hot Topics: Recent Advances in Immunology and Infectious Diseases (3ECTS)
You make one paper presentation and then you have 3 credits. Easy. And you avoid an extra exam at the end of the semester.

- Transgenic and Stem Cell Biotechnology (5 ECTS) 
Super interesting (and a little disgusting). I really recommend it!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really recommend the sport clubs though Zentrale Hochschule Sport (ZHS). It is very cheap and a wonderful way of meeting 'locals'. Be aware of the early registration opening. It was the week before the courses began.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There is many kind of sports club. I took beach volley and High Intensity Functional Training. 

Then there is Erasmus Student Network (ESN), that is run by students for international students. They have some introduction weeks (Party animals and Cultural Creatures) that are really nice.

MESA is like ESN but for TUM and the other university in Munich (LMU).

Plenty of other stuff. I seriously couldn't keep track of all the stuff going on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Hiking in the Alps. It's easy to go for a day trip. Expect at least two hours of train to get there.

There is the Deutschland Ticket for 29€/month, that works for all public transport (except long distance trains). It makes it very easy and cheap to explore the region and go hiking.

There is a climbing hall in Freising.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Hiking in the Alps. It's easy to go for a day trip. Expect at least two hours of train to get there.

There is the Deutschland Ticket for 29€/month, that works for all public transport (except long distance trains). It makes it very easy and cheap to explore the region and go hiking.

There is a climbing hall in Freising.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. People in Freising are open and super helpful

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The sport clubs, the climbing hall, the Bierfesten, the calisthenic areas... you meet people everywhere.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
My landlady was super strict and loves rules. The contract was many many pages long and I initially wasn't allowed to have my boyfriend visiting me more than two nights. I got it changed, but it was a challenge. I had several conflicts with her, where she felt 'abused' by stuff, that I did, that is very normal to do in Denmark.

By the way, it is Bavaria and people speak German. Not so much English. It is a good way of learning the language, but annoying when you have to do administrative stuff and go to the doctor.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Bavaria is a stereotype of itself. People actually wear their Dirdln and Lederhosen. And they do drink liters of beers, eat sausages and Prezels and play horn music for social events.-

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Try the sportsclubs

- Don't stress about the course registration before you arrive to the university. When you register to a course, you don't necessarily have to take the exam too.

- People are nice. Ask them for help, if you are confused. Even the professors.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The course registration process.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: People were so kind, the locals and the other international students.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was a challenge to filter in the many social events that were going on every day. You cannot get bored.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
